title: GS Global Invests in Carbon Credit Firm Hooxi Partners - Seoul Economic Daily
content:
Takes Equity Stake in Hooxi Partners, Builds Strategic Partnership
Targets Full Value Chain From Credit Sourcing to Brokerage and Trading
Seeks Synergy With Electric Bus and Renewable Energy Businesses
Accelerates Search for Overseas Carbon Reduction Projects GS Global (001250.KS) is entering the carbon credit business in earnest through a partnership with Hooxi Partners, a company specializing in carbon emission credits. The trading house plans to turn greenhouse gas reductions achieved through its existing eco-friendly operations into assets, and to expand into credit trading and brokerage by combining its global network and trading capabilities. GS Global said on the 20th that it had made an equity investment in Hooxi Partners and established a foundation for strategic cooperation. The investment is a pre-emptive move ahead of South Korea's fourth emissions trading scheme, which runs from this year through 2030. With companies facing heavier burdens in securing credits and greater price volatility as the total emissions cap shrinks, paid allocations expand and global carbon regulations tighten, GS Global aims to develop carbon credits into a new growth engine. The company said it would build capabilities in developing carbon credit methodologies and in identifying and operating reduction projects, strengthening the basis for commercializing carbon assets over the medium to long term. Hooxi Partners, founded in 2021, is a climate technology company that handles the entire process from developing carbon credit methodologies to identifying and operating reduction projects, securing Korean Offset Credits (KOCs) and forward trading. It has drawn market attention for its focus on "program-based reduction projects" in the transport sector, which bundle multiple individual projects under single management to efficiently generate reduction credits from the shift to electric vehicles. Its revenue jumped from 200 million won in 2024 to 3.2 billion won in 2025, and it is projected to post revenue of 7.8 billion won and net profit of 3.3 billion won this year. GS Global aims to maximize synergy with its existing eco-friendly businesses following the equity investment. The company plans to identify additional greenhouse gas reduction projects in areas including the conversion of internal combustion engine vehicles to electric buses, solar and other renewable energy, biomass and resource recycling, then turn those reductions into KOC assets and establish a revenue model supplying them to buyers at home and abroad. The company is also accelerating its push into overseas markets. GS Global plans to win more carbon reduction project orders from overseas clients by adding Hooxi Partners' reduction expertise to its existing network of steel, energy and industrial goods customers abroad. "This investment is intended to enter the expanding carbon credit market pre-emptively and secure a new area of growth," a GS Global official said. "Through cooperation with Hooxi Partners, we will strengthen our capabilities in securing and trading credits and continue to broaden the scope of our partnership into carbon reduction projects at home and abroad." Immersion cooling involves submerging electronic components, including GPUs and CPUs, directly in a specialized electrically non-conductive cooling fluid to remove heat. title: OPM Finalizes Rule Eliminating Time-in-Grade For GS Promotions - FedSmith.com
content: OPM has ended the 52-week time-in-grade wait for GS promotions. Here is what changes and what does not. The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) has finalized a rule eliminating the governmentwide time-in-grade requirement, a restriction that generally made General Schedule (GS) employees wait 52 weeks at a lower grade before they could be considered for promotion. The change takes effect January 19, 2027. The final rule adopts OPM’s May proposed rule substantially unchanged. However, the details show that the end of time-in-grade will not automatically mean faster promotions. The restriction applied to competitive service GS positions at GS-6 and above. A candidate generally needed 52 weeks in a position one grade lower than the job being filled or two grades lower for certain positions in occupations that advance in two-grade steps. It did not apply to Federal Wage System employees, pay-banded positions, most excepted service employees or applicants hired through open competitive examination. The requirement dates to the Whitten Amendment of the early 1950s and survived as a regulation after the underlying statutory requirement ended in 1978. OPM Director Scott Kupor said in a statement, “The old rule made the calendar a gatekeeper. If someone is qualified and ready to take on more responsibility, the government shouldn’t make them wait another year just because the clock says so.” For many employees, perhaps not right away. OPM noted in the rule that its governmentwide qualification standards have historically included a comparable one-year service period. In OPM’s words, time-in-grade “largely duplicated” a requirement imposed elsewhere. OPM says it is separately reviewing that requirement, including whether qualification should be measured by elapsed time at all. Until that review produces changes, an employee moving up a standard career ladder may find the practical timeline looks much the same. OPM cited comments from employees who said time-in-grade held them back despite relevant experience, including: Yes. Agencies may set their own job-related prerequisites, including a minimum period in grade, through their written merit promotion plans, provided the requirements are applied consistently. OPM also confirmed that eliminating time-in-grade does not require agencies to accelerate career ladder promotions. OPM set the effective date 90 days out to give agencies time to update their merit promotion plans, which may involve bargaining with unions. Until an agency revises its plan, the existing plan remains in effect minus the time-in-grade restriction. The rule also drops the requirement for OPM approval of training agreements that allowed accelerated promotions, along with the limit of two promotions in 52 weeks under those agreements. OPM tied the change directly to its new performance appraisal rule finalized in July, which allows a standardized, or forced, distribution of performance ratings. OPM said limiting top ratings will make them a more meaningful signal of which employees are ready for higher-graded work. However, OPM stated that a rating of record is neither required nor sufficient for promotion. Agencies may also weigh demonstrated results, technical assessments, structured interviews and assessments of an employee’s potential. OPM said removing the waiting period supports its effort to make federal service more competitive for early-career talent, which it is also pursuing through its Early Careers Initiative and U.S. Tech Force. In a blog post, Kupor wrote that only about 7% of the federal workforce is early career, compared with roughly 22% to 23% of the broader American workforce. This is not OPM’s first attempt. The agency proposed eliminating time-in-grade in 1994, 1995 and 2008, and finalized a rule in late 2008 before withdrawing it in 2009 pending a broader review that was never completed. OPM received 75 comments, most of them supportive. A minority argued the 52-week wait served as an objective check against managers fast-tracking favored employees. OPM responded that time-in-grade never measured whether a candidate was qualified and that merit promotion rules, which require job-related criteria and documentation, still govern selections. It declined requests for mandatory review boards, public reporting and a delayed effective date. The most immediate effect is likely to fall on employees with outside or nontraditional experience, and on agencies that want to move them up faster. For everyone else, the development to watch is OPM’s review of the one-year service-period requirement in its qualification standards, which could determine whether promotions speed up across the board. © 2026 Ian Smith. Mikaela Shiffrin (USA/Atomic) swerving some Slaloms, Lucas Pinheiro Braathen (BRA/Atomic) targeting the Super G and Lara Gut-Behrami (SUI) cheering on from the sidelines as 22-year-old Emma Aicher (GER/Head) looks to take over; welcome to the exciting new world of the 2027 Audi FIS Alpine Ski World Cup season. It has been a wildly eventful seven months since the planet’s finest last took to the slopes. Here is everything you need to know as we count down until the curtain raiser in Sölden, Austria this weekend, 24-25 October, with the FIS Alpine Skiing World Championships shining like a jewel in February 2027. From the moment she made her maiden tour appearance as a 15-year-old in Spindleruv Mlyn in 2011, Shiffrin has hogged the headlines. But now the most successful World Cup skier of all time has grabbed centre stage not for what she is doing on the slopes, but for decisions she has taken off them. For the first time since that teenage debut, Shiffrin will rarely be seen on Slalom skis this season. Instead, the woman who secured a record-extending ninth World Cup Slalom Globe in March will place her primary focus on the Giant Slalom and the Super G, two disciplines in which she has long been short of her best. It is an electrifying development that throws up an almost endless list of fascinating questions. Just two years after suffering PTSD following a heavy crash in Killington, can Shiffrin rediscover the form that made her the most successful women’s World Cup GS skier to date? Can she find the speed to challenge in the Super G, a discipline in which she has not won since December 2022? Who will step into Shiffrin’s place in the Slalom? What does all this mean for the Overall Globe? Fans will get their first answers when the American superstar takes on Sölden’s famous Rettenbach Glacier on Saturday, with the first run of the women’s GS kicking off at 10:00 CET. Shiffrin will then skip the traditional Slalom season openers in Levi and Gurgl - races she has won a combined 11 times - heading back to North America instead to focus on more GS in Killington and Tremblant, and then the speed events kicking off in Beaver Creek. Add on the fact that the season will open without Gut-Behrami, Sofia Goggia (ITA/Atomic), Federica Brignone (ITA/Rossignol) and Lindsey Vonn (USA/Head) – a quartet that boasts 198 World Cup wins between them – and it is no wonder intrigue levels are at their maximum. While Gut-Behrami has called time on her remarkable career, Goggia is hoping to have recovered from a pair of viral infections in time to start her defence of the Super G Globe in Beaver Creek, USA 11-13 December. Brignone will likely join her compatriot to train in North America but is unlikely to be ready to race. The 36-year-old had a further operation in August to remove a metal plate and screws from her leg and has barely put on skis since securing her stunning Olympic double. Vonn has been named in the wider USA ski team, but no date has been put on a possible comeback. A fifth icon, Petra Vlhova (SVK/Rossignol) is back however, ready to put smiles on faces. The 2022 Olympic Slalom champion will race in Sölden for the first time in three years after a challenging time blighted by injury. Three of those hoping to etch their name on the Overall Globe for the first time, Aicher, Camille Rast (SUI/Head) and Alice Robinson (NZL/Head) will be looking to jump ahead from the Sölden gun. If it is the German who continues her improvement in the GS – she landed her first two top-10s in the discipline in 2026 – then the others better watch out. Three wins in the Super G and two in the Downhill, plus five Slalom podiums, all in the past 18 months, surely places Aicher as the favourite to go one better than last season and succeed Shiffrin as the Big Globe champion. Rast may disagree. The only person other than Shiffrin to win a World Cup Slalom last season is primed to take full advantage of the American’s absence. The huge strides Rast took in the GS last season – a first win and top six finishes in eight out of 10 races – could be crucial too. A World Championships in her hometown of Crans-Montana also makes the Swiss star a favourite to defend her Slalom gold. Two years after becoming New Zealand’s first ever World Championship medal winner with silver in the GS, Robinson will hoping to go one better on Swiss snow. And, like her rivals, Robinson is now a real threat in more than one discipline. The GS wunderkid won last season’s SG opener in St Moritz, before following up with two second places in her next four races. While those three seem in prime position to step up, Laura Pirovano’s (ITA/Head) shock emergence showed nothing is predictable in ski racing. In early February the Italian had never been on a World Cup podium before, six weeks later she was Downhill champion, having won twice in two days in Val di Fassa and then, with everything on the line, producing one of the skis of the season at the World Cup Finals. Can she produce more of the same? Will reigning Olympic and world Downhill gold medallist Breezy Johnson (USA/Atomic) win a World Cup race? Can Julia Scheib (AUT/Rossignol) keep the Austrian smiles – and beer – flowing in Sölden with another season-setting GS victory? Talking of calendars, there are some riveting new stops to check out on the Audi World Cup tour this season, as well as returns to some favourite locations. The Austrian Alps are always the place to be during holiday season, but Dachstein West / Gosau may take that to new levels 28-29 December, with a women’s GS and Slalom ready to wow the crowds. That is not it for the Austrians, with Flachau getting a new year GS night race on 4 January, to go with the iconic starry-skied Slalom a night later. In a similar vein, the men will go in a new night Slalom in Alta Badia, alongside the popular GS. Elsewhere, Cortina and Lenzerheide are back on the women’s circuit, while the men’s tech skiers will go in Are, Sweden for the first time. Pinheiro Braathen will be among those looking to celebrate in Are. Although fascinatingly, the Brazilian will not only be seen on the short skis this winter. Months after beating Marco Odermatt (SUI/Stöckli) to both the Olympic and World Cup GS titles, Pinheiro Braathen is targeting “two missing pieces”. The first is taking the Big Globe from the Swiss man’s grasp. To do that Pinheiro Braathen knows he needs to start scoring points in a third discipline, the Super G. It will not be easy. Pinheiro Braathen has only ever started three World Cup Super G races. But having already landed Brazil a first ever Olympic medal and World Cup gong – and targeting the nation a first World Championship gold in February next year – the 26-year-old is used to defying expectation. The challenges to Odermatt’s reign will come thick and fast. Loic Meillard (SUI/Rossignol) is one of the men’s form skiers. Current Olympic and world Slalom champion, Meillard has finished second twice and third once in the past three GS Globe races. If he can start the season a little hotter – last time out it took until mid-December before he secured a first podium – the Rossignol man will challenge. Like his compatriot, Franjo von Allmen (SUI/Head) will head to Crans-Montana to defend World Championship gold. The young speedster has already shown he can do it on the biggest stages of all – three Olympic and two World titles – can he now do it week-in-week-out? Not that Odermatt will be quaking in his ski boots just yet. So dominant has the Stöckli skier been for so long that it is easy to overlook just how good he was last season. A fifth successive Overall crown, alongside the Downhill and Super G Globes and a second in the GS is seriously impressive. In fact, Odermatt has won 16 of 20 Globes he has competed for in the past five seasons. Although, a return of one gold (2025 Super G World Championships) and two silvers from his past two major championships, may mean Odi will prioritise Crans-Montana as the place to once again assert his authority. A longed-for win down the Streif in the Hahnenkamm Downhill on 23 January will also surely be circled in the diary. Unlike the women’s side, there is a fairly settled feeling to the men’s line-ups. Icons Dominik Paris (ITA/Nordica) – fresh from securing an Olympic bronze down his slope in Bormio – and Henrik Kristoffersen (NOR/Head) are back. Both will chase yet more glory. As will Clement Noël (FRA/Dynastar). The 2022 Olympic Slalom champion found a level of consistency last season (nine top 10s in 11 races) that if matched with even a proportion of the wins from previous seasons will mean a first Globe is in sight. Not that reigning Slalom World Cup champ Atle Lie McGrath (NOR/Head) will give his gong up easily. In the sad absence of Aleksander Aamodt Kilde (NOR/Atomic) who ruptured his Achilles tendon during pre-season in Chile, Italy’s new sensation Giovanni Franzoni (Rossignol) will join those looking to loosen Odermatt’s grip on the speed races. Excitingly, he will be joined by Marco Schwarz (AUT/Atomic). While not quite at Shiffrin’s level, the great Austrian all-rounder has surprised the Slalom world by deciding to hang up his short skis. Globe winner in 2021, Schwarz will pour all his energy into the Downhill, the Super G and the GS – starting in Sölden.

title: GS Securities implements Acuity AI trading signals - FX News Group
content: Acuity Trading, the AI-driven market intelligence provider for brokers and trading platforms, has announced that Dubai based CFDs broker GS Securities will be providing its clients the full Acuity intelligence suite. GS Securities clients now get AI trading signals on forex, gold and indices, a calendar of the economic and corporate events that move markets, and news and sentiment analysis, all inside one account. The agreement covers Acuity’s three intelligence pillars, Trade Intelligence, Event Intelligence and Market Intelligence, together with Market Companion, powered by MarketReader, which explains in plain language what may be driving a market move. Trade Intelligence, built on Acuity’s AnalysisIQ, combines AI with the work of Acuity’s technical analysts. Every trade idea comes with an entry level, a stop-loss, a target and the reasoning behind it, and ideas are created or updated every 10 minutes. Clients find them in the GS Securities client portal and in MT5 on desktop, so they can go from idea to order without leaving their platform. Event Intelligence tracks the developments that move prices, from economic data releases and central bank decisions to company earnings. Market Intelligence analyses news and market sentiment to show how the mood around an asset is changing and why prices may be reacting. Acuity’s Market Companion draws on price action, news, macroeconomic data and relationships between assets to explain the likely drivers behind a move. Where relevant, it shows Acuity’s analysis of the same market alongside the explanation. AI-generated content is clearly labelled. For GS Securities, the partnership adds a research layer to its MT5 offering. Clients can check the reasoning behind a trade idea, see which events are coming up and understand why a market is moving before they decide whether, and how, to trade. Andrew Lane, CEO of Acuity Trading and MarketReader, said, “Market information is most useful when traders understand the context around it. Our partnership with GS Securities puts market explanations, event intelligence and analyst-supported trade ideas in front of its clients, helping them form their own view of what is happening in the markets. “Market Companion adds to that context by explaining the potential drivers behind price movements. Together, these tools are designed to support research and individual judgement.” “Our clients want more than a price chart. They want to know why a market is moving, what is coming up next and the thinking behind a trade idea. Partnering with Acuity Trading puts that research straight into their GS Securities account, covering market movements, key events and trade ideas. “We are giving our clients better tools, not promises. Every idea shows its entry, stop-loss, target and reasoning, so clients can judge it for themselves and decide what fits their own circumstances and trading.” The Acuity intelligence suite is available now to verified GS Securities clients through the client portal and MT5 on desktop. Acuity Trading provides AI-driven market, event and trade intelligence for brokers, trading platforms and financial institutions. Its white-label technology helps firms deliver structured market insights, sentiment analysis, economic event intelligence and trade ideas across multiple channels and trading environments. All WWD content is protected by applicable copyright and intellectual property laws. The upcoming Air Jordan 3 style features a fur liner and holiday-themed graphics. News of a Santa-themed Air Jordan 3 scheduled for holiday 2026 first emerged in January and now, a first look at the sneaker has surfaced alongside confirmed release date details. As expected, the upcoming kids-exclusive Air Jordan 3 Retro style will feature a Christmas-inspired University Red/White/Gym Red colorway which includes details from a classic Air Jordan holiday ad. The shoe uses a red leather upper with darker red nubuck overlays at the toe and heel in place of the Air Jordan 3’s traditional elephant print detailing. White accents fill in both the midsole, tongue, and eyestay while the heel Jumpman Air logo is colored gold. Unique to this Air Jordan 3 colorway is a synthetic fur liner and a custom graphic insole depicting an Air Jordan 1 sneaker coming down a chimney, a reference to an original 1985 Nike, Inc. holiday advertisement. While bold in its coloring, the new Santa style isn’t the first time Michael Jordan’s classic Air Jordan 3 has been given a predominantly red makeover. Nike’s 2020 NBA All-Star Weekend collection saw the release of a Chicago-inspired “Unite” colorway which also featured a red leather upper. One of the model’s most coveted styles, the Doernbecher, which was released in 2010 and again in 2013, also used a red-based design. In other holiday-related Air Jordan news, Nike released Saturday a new Air Jordan 5 Retro Halloween style featuring glow-in-the-dark details. And while this Air Jordan 3 Santa is a grade school exclusive, another holiday-themed Air Jordan 3 dubbed “Not Nice” will be released in adult sizes. The Air Jordan 3 Retro GS Santa will be released Nov. 21 for a retail price of $155 from nike.com and select Jordan Brand retailers. The upcoming sneaker’s style code is DM0967-601.
